title: Monster Galaxy Lacks a Bright Core
caption: Giant elliptical galaxy A2261-BCG in the cluster Abell 2261, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Abell 2261, A2261-BCG · constellation Hercules · about 3 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, M. Postman (STScI), T. Lauer (NOAO), and the CLASH team

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: The giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of this Hubble image outweighs and outshines every other member of the galaxy cluster Abell 2261, three billion light-years away in Hercules. Known as A2261-BCG, it spans a little more than one million light-years, about 10 times the diameter of the Milky Way.

Astronomers expected a concentrated peak of light at its centre, marking a central black hole and the stars around it. Instead, Hubble found starlight spread fairly evenly, filling a diffuse core about 10,000 light-years across. That is the largest core yet seen, and more than three times larger than the centres of other very luminous galaxies.

Two explanations have been proposed. A pair of merging black holes may have stirred up the stars and flung them outward. Or the merged black hole may have been kicked out of the centre altogether, leaving the stars without an anchor so they spread out even more.

understand.summary: Combines visible and infrared images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. ACS F435W and F475W are shown in blue, F606W, F625W and F775W in green, and ACS F814W and F850LP with WFC3 F105W, F110W, F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: About 13 hours of exposure, much of it in infrared light invisible to the eye, gathers far more light than an eye could.

explore: In the second scenario, a merger of black holes of unequal mass could radiate gravitational waves more strongly in one direction, giving the combined black hole a kick of millions of miles an hour. At the time of the release the team was observing it again with the Very Large Array, a radio telescope in New Mexico, to pin down the black hole, if it exists. Abell 2261 is part of the CLASH survey of 25 massive galaxy clusters.
